analysis.body:
# Banking

According to the Census Bureau's latest Business to Owners Survey, 40.0% of finance and insurance firms reported using AI in the preceding two weeks, up from 36.8% in the prior period. This adoption measure reflects a sector already shaped by decades of regulatory infrastructure around quantitative models. The Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, established supervisory requirements that predate the current AI boom by more than a decade, meaning banks approach new AI deployments within an existing framework of governance that credit and anti-money laundering models have long operated under.

The frontier of AI deployment in banking has shifted from traditional credit and fraud detection toward generative AI applications in customer service and compliance functions. Financial models tuned for text processing and financial analysis have proliferated on open-source platforms, reflecting vendor and research interest in the space. Model risk rules that already govern credit and AML systems now extend oversight to newer AI applications, embedding compliance into technology selection and deployment rather than treating governance as a separate function.

Treasury has mapped the risk surface of AI in financial services, framing the supervisory conversation around use cases, opportunities, and risks. The Treasury's positioning emphasizes a coordinated regulatory approach informed by both domestic and international perspectives on how AI systems interact with financial crime detection, sanctions compliance, and corruption prevention. This whole-of-government stance reflects recognition that AI in banking extends beyond internal efficiency into the sector's role in detecting and deterring illicit cross-border financial flows.

For institutions considering AI deployment, the existing regulatory apparatus means governance is not optional and not novel. Any material AI model deployed in credit decisions, risk assessment, or compliance must satisfy model risk management standards developed over more than a decade of Fed oversight. Organizations tracking their AI maturity against public benchmarks like the Evident AI Banking Index score themselves on talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency across dozens of quantitative metrics, providing visibility into how peers approach implementation.

The regulatory posture in banking is permissive toward AI adoption but prescriptive about governance. The sector has moved past the question of whether to use AI to the question of how to manage it safely under rules already in place. This clarity, while creating overhead, also reduces regulatory uncertainty that slows deployment in less-regulated sectors.
